p: Every Saturday morning, Elif goes to the village market with her mother. The market opens at seven o'clock, and they like to arrive early because the vegetables are fresh and there are not many people. Elif does not like to wake up early on school days, but on Saturdays she is always ready before her mother.

First, they buy vegetables. Her mother likes to choose every tomato and pepper carefully, and she never buys anything before she checks the price at two or three stands. Today they buy two kilos of tomatoes, some green peppers and a big cabbage. The farmer, Mr. Hasan, always puts an extra lemon in their bag and says, "This one is a present for the best customers."

Then Elif's mother talks to the cheese seller for a long time. They talk about the weather, the prices and their children. She always buys a small piece of white cheese and some olives for breakfast. Elif waits next to her and looks at the colourful scarves at the next stand, but her mother says they do not need a new scarf.

Elif's favourite place is the bread stand. The baker is a kind old man, and he gives her a warm piece of bread every week. She eats it slowly while they walk through the market. It smells so good that other children look at her with hungry eyes!

At ten o'clock they walk home with two heavy bags. Elif carries the lighter one with the bread and the lemons. She is tired but happy. In the afternoon, her mother cooks a big lunch for the whole family, and Elif's grandfather and two uncles come to eat with them. After lunch, everybody sits in the garden and drinks tea.

p: Last month, a new family moved into the flat next to ours. The father is a doctor at the city hospital and the mother teaches music at a primary school. They have a ten-year-old son called Can and a small brown dog named Pamuk. On the first day, I saw many boxes in the corridor and a big piano that four men carried up the stairs.

At first, I was a little shy, so I only said hello when we met in the lift. Can also looked shy and he only smiled. I wanted to talk to him, but I did not know what to say. My mother said, "Give them some time. Moving to a new place is not easy."

Then one rainy evening, somebody knocked on our door. It was Can. His dog had run away through the open door, and he was very worried. He asked if we had seen Pamuk. I took my coat and an umbrella, and we looked for the dog together. We checked the garden, the car park and the small street behind our building.

Finally, we found Pamuk under a bench behind the building. He was wet and afraid of the thunder. Can took him in his arms and said thank you about five times. We walked home together, and my mother made hot chocolate for both of us.

Now Can and I play football in the garden every weekend, and Pamuk always runs after the ball. Can's mother also gives my younger sister piano lessons on Tuesdays. Last week, they invited our family for dinner. I am very happy that we have such nice neighbours, and I am glad that I did not stay shy.

p: On Monday, Murat took the bus to work as usual. It was a very crowded bus, and he had to stand all the way. He read the news on his phone for a few minutes, and then he put it in his jacket pocket. When he got off the bus at the city centre, he was thinking about an important meeting at nine o'clock.

When he arrived at his office, he put his hand in his pocket and his phone was not there. He felt cold and a bit sick. All his photos, his work emails and the phone numbers of his friends and family were on it. He looked in his bag and under his desk, but he could not find it.

Then he had an idea. He called his own number from the office phone. Nobody answered at first. He tried again, and then a third and a fourth time. After the fifth call, a woman picked up. "Hello?" she said. "Is this your phone? I found it on the seat of the bus. I was just going to take it to the police station."

Murat was so happy that he could not speak for a moment. They agreed to meet at a small café near the bus stop during his lunch break. The woman, who was called Selma, was a nurse and she was going to work in the afternoon.

At the café, Murat thanked her many times and wanted to give her some money, but she said no. "I know how it feels to lose something important," she said with a smile. "A few years ago, someone found my bag and returned it. Now it is my turn." Murat bought her a coffee and a piece of cake instead. That afternoon, he sent a message to all his friends: "Always put a password on your phone, and sometimes there are still good people in the world."

p: Most adults need between seven and nine hours of sleep every night, but many people sleep much less than that. Modern life is busy: we work late, we answer messages in bed and we watch "just one more" episode of our favourite series. Scientists say that this habit can be a serious problem, because sleep is not a waste of time. It is an active and necessary process.

When we sleep, our body repairs itself. The muscles recover after a hard day, and the immune system, which protects us from illness, becomes stronger. At the same time, the brain is busy too. It sorts the information that we received during the day, keeps the important parts and deletes the rest. This is why students who sleep well usually remember more than students who stay up all night before an exam.

A lack of sleep has clear effects on our behaviour. People who sleep badly find it harder to concentrate, and they make more mistakes at work or at school. They are also more likely to feel angry, nervous or sad. Some studies even show that tired drivers can be as dangerous as drivers who have drunk alcohol. In the long term, regular lack of sleep may increase the risk of serious illnesses such as heart disease.

So how can we sleep better? Experts suggest a few simple habits. First, go to bed and wake up at the same time every day, even at weekends. Second, avoid coffee and other strong drinks in the evening, because the effect of caffeine can last for many hours. Third, turn off your phone and television about an hour before bed, because the bright light of a screen tells the brain that it is still daytime. Finally, make your bedroom dark, quiet and slightly cool.

These small changes do not cost anything, but they can make a big difference. Many people who try them say that after only two weeks they feel more energetic and in a better mood. Perhaps the best advice is the simplest: treat sleep as an important part of your day, not as something you do when everything else is finished.

p: Istanbul is one of the few cities in the world that is on two continents. A ferry ride across the Bosphorus takes only twenty minutes, but you go from Europe to Asia. Many visitors say that this is the best way to see the city, and a ticket costs less than a cup of coffee in some countries. If you stand outside on the deck, the seagulls will follow the boat, and you will see old wooden houses, palaces and fortresses on both sides of the water.

Most tourists start their visit in the old part of the city, Sultanahmet. There you can visit the Hagia Sophia and the Blue Mosque, which are only a short walk from each other. Both buildings are more than a thousand years old, but the Blue Mosque is younger than the Hagia Sophia. Early in the morning the queues are shorter, so it is a good idea to go before nine o'clock. Remember to wear comfortable shoes, because you will walk a lot, and women should take a scarf to cover their hair when they enter a mosque.

After sightseeing, most tourists are hungry. A traditional Turkish breakfast is a good idea at any time of the day: white cheese, olives, eggs, honey, tomatoes and endless glasses of tea. For lunch you can try a fish sandwich near the Galata Bridge, where fishermen stand next to each other with their rods all day long. In the evening, many people climb the Galata Tower to watch the sunset over the Golden Horn.

If you have extra time, the Grand Bazaar is worth a visit. It has more than four thousand shops, and it is easy to get lost inside. The sellers usually expect you to bargain, so do not accept the first price you hear. Be polite, smile and offer about half of the price; the seller will probably laugh and give a better offer. Even if you do not buy anything, the colours, the smells and the sounds of the bazaar are an experience that you will remember for a long time.

Finally, a short piece of advice: do not try to see everything. Istanbul is too big for one weekend. Choose a few places, walk slowly, sit in a small café and watch the people. Most visitors who come once want to come back.

t: The Power of a Daily Walk
p: Doctors often say that walking is one of the simplest ways to stay healthy. You do not need special clothes or expensive equipment, you do not have to pay a membership fee, and you can do it almost anywhere. Just thirty minutes of fast walking a day can help your heart, control your weight and make your legs and bones stronger.

Walking is good for the mind as well. Many writers and scientists have said that they get their best ideas while walking. The German philosopher Nietzsche even wrote that "all truly great thoughts are conceived while walking". When we move, more blood goes to the brain, and we often feel calmer and more creative. A short walk outside can also reduce stress after a difficult day at work or school, especially if you walk in a park or near trees.

Of course, many people say, "I don't have time." This is a common excuse, but there are many ways to add more steps to a normal day. You can get off the bus one stop earlier, take the stairs instead of the lift, or walk while you talk on the phone. Some people hold "walking meetings" with colleagues instead of sitting in a closed room. Others walk to the shops instead of driving.

If thirty minutes sounds like too much, you can start with ten minutes and slowly increase the time. It is better to walk a little every day than to walk for three hours once a month. Wearing comfortable shoes is the only thing that really matters, because painful feet can quickly kill your motivation. A small notebook or a step counter on your phone can also help, since seeing your progress makes you proud.

Over a few weeks, you will probably notice that you sleep better, climb stairs without getting out of breath and have more energy in the afternoon. Many people also discover new streets, shops and views in their own neighbourhood. So tomorrow, why not put on your shoes and take the first step?

p: Ten years ago, people who wanted to learn a language usually had to attend classes at a school. They bought a heavy textbook, travelled to the classroom twice a week and listened to a teacher for two hours. Today, thousands of apps and websites offer lessons that you can follow at home, on the bus or during your lunch break. This makes learning cheaper and more flexible, but it also brings some new problems.

The biggest problem is motivation. When nobody is waiting for you in a classroom, it is very easy to skip a lesson. Many learners start with great energy, buy a yearly subscription and study every day for the first week. After two or three weeks, however, they are tired or busy, and slowly they stop. Studies show that most people give up an online course before they finish it.

How can we avoid this? First, set a small daily goal. Learning five new words every day sounds easy, but after a year it means almost two thousand words. Second, connect your lessons with a fixed time, for example, right after breakfast or just before you go to bed. A habit that is tied to another habit is easier to keep. Third, find a friend or a group who study the same language, because it is more difficult to stop when others are waiting for you.

Another important challenge is speaking practice. Apps are very good for vocabulary and grammar, and many of them use games to make learning fun. However, a game cannot give you a real conversation. In real life, people speak fast, use slang and make jokes that are not in the book. To improve your speaking, you need to talk to real people. Language exchange groups and online conversation partners are a great solution because they are often free, and both sides help each other.

In the end, the best method is a mixture. Use an app for a daily routine, read short texts or stories at your level, listen to podcasts or songs, and speak with other people whenever you can. Do not be afraid of mistakes; they are a normal and necessary part of learning. The only real mistake is to stop.

p: Since the pandemic, working from home has become normal for millions of employees around the world. Supporters argue that it saves commuting time, reduces costs and allows people to organise their day more flexibly. A parent can take a child to school and then start work, and an employee who lives far from an expensive city centre can find a good job without moving. Many companies have also noticed that some staff are more productive when they are not constantly interrupted by colleagues in a busy open-plan office.

The environmental argument is also often mentioned. Fewer people travelling to work means less traffic, less pollution and lower fuel consumption. Some firms have even reduced the size of their offices and saved large amounts of rent, which they can invest in training or higher salaries.

However, remote work is not suitable for everyone. Some employees complain that the boundary between work and private life disappears: they answer emails late at night, eat lunch in front of the computer and find it difficult to switch off. Young employees, who have less experience, often miss the chance to learn by watching more senior colleagues, and they sometimes feel invisible when promotions are discussed. Others feel lonely because they miss the casual conversations that happen in the corridor or at the coffee machine. Psychologists warn that long-term isolation can increase anxiety and reduce creativity, as good ideas often appear during informal exchanges.

Managers face challenges too. It is much harder to build a team spirit through a screen, and some bosses do not trust their staff when they cannot see them. This sometimes leads to excessive monitoring, with software that records every click of the mouse, which employees find stressful and insulting. Experts believe that managers should judge people by the results of their work, not by the number of hours they spend online.

As a result, a growing number of organisations are choosing a hybrid model, in which staff spend part of the week in the office and the rest at home. In this system, the office becomes a place for meetings, teamwork and social contact, while quiet, concentrated tasks are done at home. Whether this compromise will last remains to be seen, but it suggests that most people want both independence and human contact.

p: Electric cars were once seen as expensive toys for people who cared about the environment. Twenty years ago, they were slow, they could travel only a short distance, and there was almost nowhere to charge them. Today they are becoming a mainstream choice. Prices have fallen, the distance a car can travel on one charge has more than doubled, and more charging stations are appearing in cities, at shopping centres and along motorways.

Drivers who have changed to an electric car often mention practical advantages. The running costs are lower, since electricity is cheaper than petrol in most countries and the engine has far fewer moving parts that can break. The cars are very quiet, and they accelerate quickly because the motor gives full power from the very first moment. In many cities, owners also pay lower taxes or can use special parking places.

The main environmental argument is that electric cars produce no exhaust fumes, so the air in busy cities becomes cleaner and people suffer fewer breathing problems. Critics, however, point out that the electricity itself must come from somewhere. If it is produced by burning coal, the overall benefit is much smaller, because the pollution simply moves from the street to the power station. Producing the batteries also requires large amounts of energy and raw materials such as lithium and cobalt, whose mining can damage landscapes and create difficult working conditions.

Another concern is infrastructure. If millions of people charge their cars in the evening at the same time, the electricity network may not be able to cope. Engineers are therefore developing "smart charging", which automatically starts the charge when the demand is low, for example in the middle of the night. Some experiments even use the batteries of parked cars as a storage system that gives energy back to the grid when it is needed.

Despite these concerns, most experts agree that the long-term trend is clear. As more electricity comes from wind and solar power, the advantages of electric vehicles will grow. The remaining challenges are to make charging faster, to reduce the cost of batteries even further and to recycle old batteries safely. If these problems are solved, the petrol car may soon look as old-fashioned as the horse and carriage.

p: We all know the feeling: an important task is waiting, but instead we tidy our desk, check our phone for the tenth time or suddenly become very interested in cleaning the kitchen. This behaviour is called procrastination, and almost everybody does it. A famous survey suggests that about one in five adults is a chronic procrastinator, and among university students the number is even higher. Many people think it is simply laziness, but psychologists say it has very little to do with that.

Research suggests that people often delay a task not because they are idle, but because the task makes them feel uncomfortable. They may be anxious about doing it badly, bored by its detail or confused about where to begin. Avoiding the task provides a short moment of relief, and this is the problem: the brain learns that avoiding the task makes bad feelings go away, so it repeats the behaviour next time. In other words, procrastination is not a problem of time management, but of managing emotions.

The costs can be serious. People who postpone tasks often work under pressure at the last moment, make more mistakes and sleep badly. They may also feel guilty, which makes them even more reluctant to start the next time. Some studies link chronic procrastination with higher stress, weaker health and lower income, because opportunities are lost when we wait too long.

Fortunately, there are practical ways to break the cycle. Dividing a big project into very small steps makes the starting point less frightening: instead of "write the report", the first step can be "write the title and one sentence". Another popular method is to work for only twenty-five minutes and then take a five-minute break, which makes the task feel short and manageable. It also helps to remove distractions by putting the phone in another room and by telling a friend what you intend to finish today.

Most importantly, being kind to yourself after a delay works better than harsh self-criticism. In one experiment, students who forgave themselves for delaying their first exam preparation procrastinated less before the next exam than those who blamed themselves. Self-criticism tends to increase stress and lead to further delay, while self-compassion gives us the energy to try again.

o: uncomfortable feelings about the task
a lack of basic time-management skills
having too much free time at home
poor intelligence or a weak memory
q.e: "it has very little to do with laziness" ve devamı.

It makes the task much easier to do later on.
It improves the way we plan our daily time.
It makes other people do the whole job for us.
q.e: "a short moment of relief... the brain learns... repeats the behaviour."

q.q: What is one cost of procrastination mentioned in the text?
o: Working under pressure and making mistakes
Losing the ability to concentrate for long
Having less time to relax at weekends
Earning less money than colleagues do
q.e: "work under pressure at the last moment, make more mistakes and sleep badly."

q.q: What does the method of "twenty-five minutes of work and a five-minute break" try to do?
o: It makes the task feel short and manageable.
It helps people to sleep much better at night.
It replaces the need for long holidays.
It removes the need to plan the work in advance.
q.e: "makes the task feel short and manageable."

o: Students who forgave themselves delayed less.

q.e: "students who forgave themselves... procrastinated less before the next exam."

p: Conventional wisdom holds that the more options we have, the happier we are. Freedom of choice is widely regarded as one of the great achievements of modern societies: supermarkets offer dozens of kinds of bread, streaming services provide thousands of films, and online shops allow us to compare hundreds of nearly identical products at any hour of the day. Yet a growing body of research suggests that an abundance of choice can be paralysing rather than liberating.

In one well-known experiment, shoppers in a food store were offered either a small selection of jams or a very large one. The larger display attracted more attention, and more people stopped to taste the jams. But customers who saw the smaller selection were considerably more likely to buy something. Similar results have been found in studies of retirement plans, where employees confronted with many investment funds were less likely to enrol in any of them at all.

One explanation is that every additional option raises our expectations and increases the cost of a wrong decision. When we eventually choose, we are haunted by the thought that a better alternative was available, a feeling that psychologists call regret. Moreover, when something disappoints us, we have nobody to blame but ourselves; in a world with fewer options, we could attribute disappointment to circumstances. Psychologist Barry Schwartz has argued that this is one reason why levels of depression have risen in wealthy societies, even though people have more freedom than ever before.

Researchers also distinguish between two types of decision makers. "Maximisers" try to find the absolute best option and will compare every alternative before they commit. "Satisficers", on the other hand, settle for the first option that meets their needs. Surprisingly, maximisers often achieve objectively better results, such as higher-paying jobs, but they tend to be less satisfied with their decisions than satisficers, because they constantly wonder whether an even better option exists.

This does not mean that choice is inherently harmful. Rather, it implies that the quality of a decision depends on how we make it. Setting clear criteria in advance, limiting the number of alternatives we consider, and accepting that no choice is perfect can turn an overwhelming process into a manageable one. Some people even deliberately reduce their options, for example by wearing similar clothes every day, in order to save mental energy for the decisions that really matter.

o: Bigger displays drew more attention but fewer sales.
Bigger displays drew more attention and more sales.

q.e: Büyük sergi dikkat çekti ama küçük sergide satın alma olasılığı daha yüksekti.

q.e: "were less likely to enrol in any of them at all."

q.e: "every additional option raises our expectations and increases the cost of a wrong decision."

q.e: "often achieve objectively better results... but they tend to be less satisfied."

q.e: "the quality of a decision depends on how we make it."

search carefully for a better solution
q.e: settle for = (en iyisi olmasa da) yetinmek.

p: As urban populations continue to swell, city planners face a dilemma: land is scarce and expensive, yet residents increasingly demand parks and gardens. According to the United Nations, more than two thirds of the world's people will live in cities by the middle of this century, and the pressure on every square metre will grow accordingly. For a long time, green areas were regarded as a luxury that could be sacrificed whenever developers needed room for housing or offices. That view is now being challenged.

Studies indicate that access to green space is associated with lower stress levels, better physical health and stronger community ties. Patients in hospital rooms with a view of trees have been found to recover faster than patients who look at a brick wall. Parks also give children a safe place to play and elderly people a reason to leave their flats, which helps to prevent loneliness. Trees cool the surrounding air by several degrees, which is becoming vital as heatwaves grow more frequent; in some neighbourhoods, the temperature on a tree-lined street can be ten degrees lower than on a nearby asphalt road. Moreover, parks absorb rainwater, reducing the risk of flooding after heavy storms.

Critics counter that such benefits are unevenly distributed. Wealthier districts tend to enjoy leafy avenues and well-kept parks, while poorer neighbourhoods are left with concrete, noise and traffic. Researchers describe this as a form of environmental inequality, since the people who most need the cooling and cleaning effects of vegetation are often the ones who have the least access to it. Some cities have therefore adopted policies requiring that every resident live within a short walk of a park.

Creative solutions have emerged where space is limited. Planners have turned abandoned railway lines into elevated gardens, covered roofs with grass and flowers, and planted vertical forests on the sides of tall apartment blocks. In several cities, residents are even encouraged to transform unused corners of land into small community gardens, which brings neighbours together and provides fresh vegetables.

Yet a paradox remains. When a neighbourhood becomes greener and more attractive, property prices tend to rise, and this process, often called "green gentrification", can push out the very people the improvements were meant to help. Whether ambitious green targets can be met without raising housing costs, and who should pay for them, remains hotly debated.

They were cheaper to build than housing.
They were seen as a danger to public health.
q.e: "regarded as a luxury that could be sacrificed."

q.e: Arazi fiyatlarının düşmesi metinde yok.

The parks are poorly looked after.

q.e: "such benefits are unevenly distributed."

q.e: "turned abandoned railway lines into elevated gardens."

t: The Library That Changed Its Rules
p: For many years, the public library in the small town of Marlow was a very quiet place. People came in, borrowed a few books, and left. The rules were strict: no talking, no food, no phones, and a fine for every book that was returned late. The librarian, Mrs. Hughes, had worked there for thirty years, and she believed that silence was the most important thing a library could offer.

But over time, fewer and fewer people visited. The number of borrowed books fell every year, and the town council began to ask whether the building was worth its cost. Some council members even suggested closing it and selling the land. When Mrs. Hughes heard this, she was shocked. She had always thought that everybody loved the library as much as she did.

Her young assistant, Daniel, had a different idea. He had grown up in Marlow, and he remembered that as a teenager he had stopped going to the library because it felt like a place where he was always doing something wrong. 'People don't hate books,' he told her one afternoon. 'They hate feeling unwelcome.' At first Mrs. Hughes disagreed, but she agreed to try a small experiment for three months.

The first change was simple: the library removed the late fines. Instead of paying money, people who returned a book late only had to wait a few days before borrowing another one. Many families who had stopped visiting because of old debts came back. One woman cried when she was told that she no longer owed anything after six years. She returned with her three children the very next day.

The second change was a quiet room and a 'talking room'. In the quiet room, the old rules stayed the same, so students and people who wanted to read in peace could still enjoy the silence. In the talking room, however, visitors could chat, drink coffee, and even work in groups. Daniel placed a few sofas there and added a small table with free tea. Within a week, the talking room was full every afternoon.

The third change was the most surprising. The staff began to organise free events: a weekly storytelling hour for children, a computer class for older people, and a monthly evening where neighbours could swap clothes and tools. Some events were popular at once, while others took time to attract visitors. A cooking club for beginners, for example, started with only two people, but after two months, more than twenty were coming every Thursday.

Not everyone was happy. A few regular readers complained that the building had become too noisy, and Mrs. Hughes herself felt uncomfortable at first when she heard laughter near the shelves. 'It doesn't feel like a library any more,' she said. Daniel answered calmly, 'Maybe it feels like a library for more people.' She did not reply, but the next day she was seen sitting in the talking room with a cup of tea, listening to a group of teenagers discussing a novel.

After three months, the results were clear. The number of visitors had doubled, and book loans had increased by forty percent. Even better, the library now had a waiting list for its computer classes. The town council, which had planned to close the building, instead decided to give it a small budget increase. One council member said, 'We didn't realise the library was something the whole community could use.'

Today, Mrs. Hughes is retired, and Daniel is the head librarian. The quiet room still exists, and it is as peaceful as ever. But the heart of the building is the talking room, where children, students, and grandparents sit side by side. On the wall hangs a small sign that Mrs. Hughes wrote before she left: 'A library is not a place for books. It is a place for people who love stories, and stories are told in many voices.'

The story of the Marlow library shows that change does not always mean losing what is valuable. By keeping the best of the past and listening to the needs of the present, a place that seemed old-fashioned became important to the town again. Many other small libraries in the region have since visited Marlow to learn how it was done, and several of them have started similar experiments of their own.

q.e: The number of borrowed books fell every year, and the council asked whether the building was worth its cost.

q.e: 'They hate feeling unwelcome.'

q.e: People only had to wait a few days before borrowing another one.

q.e: It started with only two people, but after two months more than twenty were coming.

p: Many parents and teachers complain that teenagers are lazy in the morning. They stay in bed until noon on weekends, they look tired during the first lesson, and they often fall asleep in class. However, scientists who study sleep say that this is not simply a question of bad habits. During the teenage years, the human body goes through real changes that affect when we feel sleepy and when we feel awake.

The main reason is the biological clock, a small system in the brain that tells the body when to sleep. In children, this clock usually makes them tired around eight or nine in the evening. In teenagers, the clock moves later. The body begins to produce the hormone that makes us sleepy about two hours later than before. This means that a fifteen-year-old who is lying in bed at ten o'clock may simply not be able to fall asleep, even if he wants to.

At the same time, teenagers need a lot of sleep, usually between eight and ten hours every night. But many of them get much less. School often starts at eight o'clock or earlier, so a student who falls asleep at midnight and wakes up at six has only six hours of rest. Over a week, this lost sleep adds up, and doctors call it 'sleep debt'. Like a money debt, it has to be paid back at some point, which is why teenagers sleep so long at weekends.

The effects of too little sleep are serious. Tired students find it harder to concentrate, and they remember less of what they study. They are also more likely to feel anxious or sad, and some research suggests that they have more accidents, especially when they begin to drive. Their health suffers too: people who regularly sleep too little are more likely to gain weight and to catch colds.

Modern technology makes the problem worse. Many teenagers use their phones in bed, watching videos or chatting with friends. The screen produces a bright blue light, which tells the brain that it is still daytime. As a result, the body produces less of the sleepy hormone, and it becomes even harder to fall asleep. In addition, messages and notifications can wake young people during the night without them even realising it.

Some schools have tried a simple solution: starting lessons later. In several cities, schools moved the first lesson from eight to nine o'clock. The results were encouraging. Students were more alert in class, their marks improved slightly, and fewer of them were late. Teachers also reported that students were in a better mood and caused fewer problems. However, not everyone liked the change. Some parents said that later lessons meant a later end to the day, which made it difficult to organise sports, jobs, and family time.

What can teenagers do at home? Experts suggest a few practical steps. First, try to go to bed and get up at similar times every day, even at weekends, so that the body clock stays regular. Second, stop using screens at least an hour before bed, and keep the phone outside the bedroom if possible. Third, avoid drinks with caffeine, such as cola or energy drinks, in the afternoon and evening. Finally, make the bedroom dark, cool, and quiet.

Parents can help too. Instead of getting angry about late mornings, they can try to understand that their children are not trying to be difficult. A calm talk about sleep, together with a few agreed rules about phones in the evening, is usually more effective than punishment. Some families even choose a shared 'switch-off hour', when everyone in the house puts their devices away.

In the end, sleep is not a waste of time. It is the period when the brain stores memories, repairs the body, and prepares us for the next day. If we want young people to learn well and stay healthy, we need to take their sleep as seriously as we take their food, their exercise, and their education.

q.q: According to the passage, why are teenagers sleepy in the morning?
o: Their biological clock moves later.
They are lazier than adults are.
They eat too much late at night.
They do not enjoy going to school.
q.e: In teenagers, the clock moves later; the sleepy hormone is produced about two hours later.

q.q: What is "sleep debt"?
o: Lost sleep that adds up over several days
Money paid back for an expensive bed
A medical test for people with insomnia
A habit of sleeping too many hours
q.e: Lost sleep adds up, and doctors call it sleep debt; it has to be paid back.

q.q: How does phone light affect sleep?
o: It tells the brain it is still daytime.
It makes the body produce more sleepy hormone.
It has no effect on how people sleep.
It makes people dream much more.
q.e: The blue light tells the brain that it is still daytime.

o: Students were more alert and did slightly better.
Students became lazier and failed more exams.
Many teachers decided to leave their jobs.
Nothing changed in the results of the schools.
q.e: Students were more alert, marks improved slightly, fewer were late.

q.q: Why did some parents dislike later lessons?
o: Lessons would end later, which affected other activities.
They believed that exam marks would fall.
They wanted their children to sleep a good deal less.
School fees would have to rise every single year.
q.e: Later lessons meant a later end to the day, which made sports, jobs, and family time difficult.

o: Drink coffee in the evening to stay awake
Keep regular times for sleeping and waking
Stop using screens an hour before bed

q.e: Experts recommend avoiding caffeine in the afternoon and evening.

t: The City That Fell in Love with Bicycles
p: Twenty years ago, the city of Veldhaven was famous for one thing: traffic. Every morning, thousands of cars moved slowly towards the centre, and the air smelled of exhaust. A journey of five kilometres could take an hour. People complained, the mayor promised improvements, and nothing happened. Then a new transport director, Anneke Jansen, arrived with a plan that many people thought was crazy.

Her idea was to make cycling the easiest way to move around the city. She did not ask people to give up their cars immediately. Instead, she wanted to build a network of safe bicycle lanes, separated from cars by a low wall or a row of plants. 'Most people don't cycle because they are afraid,' she explained. 'If they feel safe, they will try it.'

The first lanes opened on two main roads, and the reaction was bad. Shop owners were angry because they thought customers would not be able to park. Drivers complained that the roads had become narrower. A local newspaper called the project 'a waste of public money', and some residents wrote letters demanding that the lanes be removed. Anneke listened to every complaint, but she did not change her plan.

Within a year, however, the picture began to change. A study counted the people who passed along the main road and found that the number of cyclists had tripled. The shops had not lost customers; in fact, they had gained some, because cyclists stopped more often than drivers and spent more time in the area. Several shop owners who were skeptical at first now asked for lanes outside their own doors.

The city also made cycling more convenient. It built large, guarded parking places near the railway station, where people could leave their bikes for a small fee. Employers were encouraged to offer showers for workers who cycled to the office. Schools organised lessons on road safety, and children who passed a simple test received a small certificate. Over time, riding a bicycle became something normal, even fashionable.

The results were measurable. Traffic jams in the city centre fell by almost a third, and the average commute became shorter, even for the drivers who stayed in their cars. Air pollution dropped, and hospitals reported fewer cases of breathing problems among children. Because people were exercising every day without really thinking about it, the city's health costs also began to fall, and an insurance company even offered lower prices to regular cyclists.

Of course, the system is not perfect. In winter, when it rains or snows, the lanes can be dangerous, and the city has to work hard to keep them clear. Some elderly residents and people with disabilities cannot cycle at all, so buses and special taxis remain very important. Anneke herself admits that the plan would not have worked without good public transport. 'Bicycles are one part of the solution, not the whole of it,' she says.

Visitors from other countries now come to Veldhaven to see how it works. Many are surprised by how calm the streets feel. Parents ride with small children on the back of their bikes, businessmen travel in suits, and old people move slowly along the lanes with shopping baskets. There is no special clothing, no race, and no hurry.

The story shows that big changes in a city often begin with a small, brave decision. Anneke Jansen was not popular at first, but she stayed patient and trusted the evidence. Today, even the shop owner who once called her plan stupid says, 'I was wrong. Veldhaven is a better place to live.'

q.e: Thousands of cars moved slowly and the air smelled of exhaust.

q.e: Build a network of safe lanes separated from cars.

q.e: They thought customers would not be able to park.

q.e: Cyclists tripled and shops had even gained some customers.

q.e: Lanes can be dangerous in winter; some elderly and disabled people cannot cycle.

q.e: The plan would not have worked without good public transport.

p: Few people today can remember the last time they spent an entire hour on a single task without checking a phone, answering a message, or opening a new browser tab. This is not entirely surprising. Modern devices and applications are designed by teams of engineers whose success is measured by how much of our time they capture. Every sound, every red badge, and every vibration is carefully tested to make us look. What is less well understood is how much this constant switching costs us.

Researchers who study attention have found that a brief interruption does far more damage than its length suggests. In one well-known experiment, office workers who were interrupted by a short message needed, on average, more than twenty minutes to return fully to their original task. Even when the interruption lasted only seconds, the mind had to rebuild its mental picture of the problem, remember where it had stopped, and recover its earlier momentum. People who were interrupted more frequently completed their work faster, but they made more mistakes and reported higher levels of stress.

The problem is not just that we are distracted; it is that we are distracting ourselves. Many interruptions come not from colleagues or family but from our own impulse to check something. Psychologists compare this behaviour to a slot machine: because a new message or a piece of news might be waiting, the habit of checking is rewarded unpredictably, which is exactly the pattern that makes habits difficult to break. After a while, the urge becomes automatic, and people may pick up their phones without even noticing.

The consequences extend beyond productivity. Deep, sustained thinking, the kind needed to write a complicated report, learn a difficult skill, or solve a technical problem, seems to depend on long periods of uninterrupted concentration. If we rarely experience such periods, our ability to produce them may weaken. Some teachers have observed that students find it increasingly hard to read long texts, not because they lack intelligence but because their minds are accustomed to jumping from one short piece of content to another. Critics call this 'shallow' thinking, although the term may be unfair to those who handle large amounts of information with great skill.

Not everyone agrees that the situation is as serious as these warnings suggest. Some scholars point out that every new communication technology, from the printing press to television, was once accused of damaging human intelligence. Moreover, the ability to switch quickly between tasks is valuable in many modern jobs, from emergency medicine to journalism. These sceptics argue that what looks like lost concentration may in fact be an adaptation to a faster environment. The evidence for long-term damage to the brain, they note, is still limited and often based on small studies.

Even so, most researchers accept that individuals can benefit from managing their attention more deliberately. A number of strategies have proved useful. The simplest is to turn off non-essential notifications, so that the device no longer decides when we look at it. Another is to work in blocks of focused time, perhaps forty-five minutes, with the phone out of sight, followed by a short break that is genuinely restful rather than filled with more screens. Some people schedule fixed times for email and social media, treating them as tasks like any other.

Employers have a role to play as well. Companies that expect an immediate reply to every message create an atmosphere in which no one can concentrate. A few organisations have experimented with 'quiet hours', during which meetings and chat messages are not allowed, and they report improvements in both the quality of work and the satisfaction of employees. The key, according to the managers involved, is that the policy comes from the top: if senior staff continue to send messages at all hours, ordinary employees will feel obliged to respond.

Ultimately, attention is a limited resource, and every society decides, usually without realising it, how to spend it. For the first time in history, a handful of private companies have a major influence on where billions of people direct their minds each day. Whether that is a healthy arrangement is a question that individuals, schools, employers, and governments will need to consider seriously. Until then, perhaps the most practical step is also the most modest: to notice, the next time the phone lights up, that we are being asked to give something valuable, and to choose whether to give it.

q.q: Why are devices designed to capture our attention, according to the first paragraph?
o: Engineers are judged by how much time they capture.
Users demand products that are hard to put down.
Governments require companies to keep users online.

q.e: Teams of engineers whose success is measured by how much of our time they capture.

p: Linguists estimate that there are roughly seven thousand languages spoken in the world today, but nearly half of them are endangered. On average, one language falls silent every few weeks, usually when its last fluent speaker dies. Because many of these languages have never been written down, they vanish without leaving a trace. The loss is easy to overlook, since it happens quietly and far from major cities, yet scholars regard it as one of the largest cultural losses of our time.

Languages rarely die because of a single dramatic event. More often, the process is gradual and takes place over three or four generations. In the first generation, adults speak the local language at home but also learn a dominant language in order to work, attend school, or deal with officials. In the second, parents begin to speak the dominant language to their children, believing it will give them better opportunities. By the third generation, the children understand their grandparents but answer in the majority language. The chain of transmission is broken, and within a few decades the language is spoken only by the elderly.

Economic and social pressures play a decisive role. When one language is associated with jobs, education, and modern life, while another is linked to poverty or a rural past, families often make a practical choice. Parents do not necessarily love their own language less; they simply do not want their children to be disadvantaged. In some places, the decision has not been entirely voluntary. Governments have at times banned minority languages in schools or punished children for using them, which created a lasting sense that speaking the old language was something to be ashamed of.

Why does it matter if a language disappears? Linguists give several answers. First, each language contains a unique way of describing the world, including detailed knowledge of local plants, animals, and landscapes that may not exist in any other form. When the speakers of a language of the rainforest are lost, for example, so may be their knowledge of medicinal plants. Second, languages are the basis of identity and heritage, carrying stories, songs, and traditions that give a community its sense of itself. Third, studying the world's diversity helps scientists understand how the human mind organises grammar and meaning.

There are, however, voices that question whether efforts to save languages are always realistic. Some argue that communities have the right to choose a language that serves them, and that outsiders who romanticise small languages may ignore the real needs of their speakers. Others point out that revival projects can be costly and that their results are uncertain. These critics do not deny the value of diversity, but they insist that preservation should never be forced on people who do not want it.

Despite these debates, some revival efforts have been remarkably successful. In New Zealand, Māori communities created 'language nests', pre-schools in which very young children were taught entirely in Māori by elders. A generation later, many of those children had become parents who spoke the language to their own families. In Wales, laws that require road signs, public services, and school lessons to include Welsh have helped to stabilise a language that once seemed likely to decline. In both cases, the key factor was not only government support but also the enthusiasm of the speakers themselves.

Technology now offers new tools. Researchers record elderly speakers on smartphones and build online dictionaries. Young people create videos, songs, and social media posts in their heritage languages, giving them a modern and attractive image. Some companies have begun to add smaller languages to their translation services, although the quality is still uneven. Such efforts cannot replace a living community of speakers, but they can slow the decline and provide material for future generations to learn from.

The central lesson of the research seems to be that a language survives only when it is used in daily life, particularly by children. Dictionaries and archives are valuable, but a language that exists only in books is more like a museum object than a means of communication. Preventing the disappearance of the world's languages will therefore require more than recording words; it will require societies that give people a real reason, and a real freedom, to keep speaking them.

p: On a summer afternoon, the narrow streets of an old European port town can be almost impossible to walk through. Groups of visitors follow guides holding umbrellas, cruise passengers fill the small squares, and the local café owner serves more customers in one hour than he once did in a day. For the tourists, the town is a charming escape. For the people who live there, it is increasingly difficult to call it home. This tension has given rise to a new word: overtourism.

Tourism is one of the world's largest industries, and for many regions it is the main source of income. It creates jobs for guides, hotel workers, drivers, and shopkeepers, and it brings foreign money that can pay for roads, museums, and the restoration of historic buildings. Before the pandemic, international arrivals had been growing steadily for decades, helped by cheap flights, online booking platforms, and a growing middle class in many countries. Some destinations saw their number of visitors multiply many times within a generation.

The costs, however, are not shared equally. Residents of popular towns report that rents have risen sharply because landlords prefer to offer short holiday lets rather than long-term homes. Teachers, nurses, and young families are driven out of the centre, and ordinary shops that sold bread and tools are replaced by souvenir stores. In some historic districts, the permanent population has fallen by half, leaving neighbourhoods that look lively during the day and empty at night. 'We are living in a theatre set,' one resident remarked.

Environmental damage is another concern. Crowds wear down ancient stones, litter collects on beaches, and boats leave pollution in fragile waters. Popular natural sites, once peaceful, now suffer from erosion because of the number of hikers. A single large cruise ship can release as much air pollution in a day as thousands of cars, and travel by plane contributes to climate change, which in turn threatens many of the places visitors come to enjoy.

Authorities have tried a variety of solutions. Some cities charge an entry fee to day visitors, hoping both to raise revenue and to discourage the most casual crowds. Others limit the number of tickets for the most famous monuments or require advance booking, so that arrivals are spread throughout the day. A few have restricted the number of holiday apartments or banned the construction of new hotels in the centre. These policies are controversial. Business owners fear that visitors will go elsewhere, while some critics argue that entry fees turn historic places into attractions that only wealthy people can afford.

Many experts believe that the answer lies not in stopping tourism but in changing its pattern. Encouraging travel outside the peak summer months would reduce pressure and provide year-round work for local people. Promoting lesser-known towns and regions could spread income more widely, instead of concentrating it in a handful of famous spots. Visitors themselves can make a difference by staying longer in fewer places, choosing locally owned accommodation, and respecting the rules and customs of the community.

There is also an argument that residents should have a stronger voice in decisions. In several places, local councils have organised public meetings and surveys to ask what kind of tourism people actually want. The results are often more moderate than expected: most residents do not wish to eliminate visitors, but they want to see more of the profits stay in their own neighbourhoods and a guarantee that housing remains affordable for those who work there.

The debate over overtourism is ultimately a question of balance. A destination that depends completely on visitors is vulnerable, as the pandemic showed when whole towns lost their income overnight. Yet a place that ignores its residents risks losing the very character that made it attractive. The most sustainable tourism, many say, is the kind that leaves a community richer, not poorer, than it found it, and in which the people who live somewhere remain welcome in their own streets.

p: Every few decades, a new wave of technology provokes the same fear: that machines will take away human work. In the early nineteenth century, textile workers destroyed looms that threatened their jobs. In the twentieth century, factory automation and computers raised similar worries. Today, advances in artificial intelligence and robotics have revived the debate, and this time the discussion includes not only factory workers but also accountants, translators, and even doctors.

History offers some reassurance, but not a guarantee. In the past, technology did destroy particular jobs, yet it also created new ones, often in areas no one had imagined. Few people in 1900 predicted that millions would one day work as software developers, flight attendants, or social media managers. Economists note that automation tends to make goods cheaper and companies more productive, which increases demand and eventually creates additional employment elsewhere. The difficulty is that this process is neither immediate nor painless. A worker in his fifties who loses a factory job cannot easily become a programmer.

What seems different about the current wave is the range of tasks that machines can learn. Earlier automation mainly replaced physical, repetitive work. Modern systems can recognise images, process language, and make predictions, abilities once considered uniquely human. As a result, some researchers estimate that a large share of existing occupations include tasks that could be partly automated. It is important to notice the word 'partly': most jobs consist of many different activities, and only some of them are routine enough to hand over to a machine.

This suggests that the more realistic scenario is not the complete replacement of workers but a change in how work is organised. A radiologist who uses software to scan thousands of images may spend less time on routine checking and more on discussing results with patients. A lawyer might use a program to search documents in minutes rather than days, leaving more time for strategy and negotiation. In these cases, technology acts as a tool that increases productivity rather than as a rival. Nevertheless, the benefits may go mainly to those who already have skills and capital, which could widen inequality.

The question for societies, then, is how to prepare. Education is the most frequently mentioned answer. If machines handle routine tasks, people will need skills that are harder to automate, such as creativity, critical thinking, and the ability to work with others. But many experts warn against simple slogans. Schools cannot predict exactly which skills will be needed in twenty years, so they argue that the most useful lesson may be how to keep learning throughout life. Governments and employers will need to fund retraining programmes, and workers will need the time and support to use them.

Others focus on protection. Some propose stronger unemployment benefits or wage subsidies for people whose jobs disappear, while a few advocate a universal basic income, a regular payment to every citizen. Supporters say that such a payment would give people security in an uncertain labour market, but opponents worry about the cost and fear that it might reduce the motivation to work. Experiments in several countries have produced mixed results, and the debate remains open.

There is also a question about who decides how technology is used. Companies often adopt automation to reduce costs, but they could equally use it to improve the quality of products or to reduce dangerous and exhausting work. Workers and unions increasingly ask to take part in these decisions, especially when systems are used to monitor performance. Without clear rules, they argue, machines may be used to make jobs more stressful rather than better.

None of this means that the future must be gloomy. Technology has already removed some of the heaviest and most dangerous tasks from human life, and it may continue to do so. But the outcome depends less on the machines themselves than on the choices societies make about education, fairness, and the sharing of benefits. As in earlier centuries, the question is not whether technology will change work, but who will be asked to adapt, and who will profit when they do.

p: The common metaphor for memory is a recording device: we imagine that experiences are stored somewhere in the brain like footage on a hard drive, to be played back when needed. Decades of psychological research have shown that this picture is deeply misleading. Remembering is not retrieval but reconstruction. Each time we recall an event, the brain assembles it afresh from fragments, filling the gaps with expectations, general knowledge, and information acquired later. The result feels vivid and authentic, yet it may differ in significant ways from what actually occurred.

The pioneering experiments of Elizabeth Loftus in the 1970s demonstrated how easily this reconstruction can be influenced. Participants who watched footage of a car accident were asked how fast the vehicles were going when they 'smashed into' each other, or alternatively when they 'hit' each other. Those who heard the more forceful verb gave higher speed estimates and, a week later, were more likely to report having seen broken glass, although none had appeared in the film. A single word, introduced after the event, had altered what people believed they had witnessed.

Subsequent studies pushed the findings further. Researchers managed to persuade a considerable proportion of volunteers that they had been lost in a shopping mall as children, an event that never happened, by presenting it alongside genuine memories supplied by relatives. Some participants not only accepted the story but elaborated it with convincing detail. The implication is unsettling: confidence and vividness, the qualities by which we usually judge our own recollections, are poor indicators of accuracy.

Nowhere are these findings more consequential than in the courtroom. Eyewitness testimony carries enormous persuasive weight, since jurors tend to trust a confident witness who describes a crime in detail. Yet analyses of cases in which convictions were later overturned by DNA evidence reveal that mistaken identification was a contributing factor in a large majority. Witnesses had, in good faith, selected the wrong person from a line-up, often because the procedure itself subtly guided them. A detective who knows the suspect's identity may inadvertently signal it through tone or expression, and a witness who is told that the culprit is 'definitely in the group' feels pressure to choose someone.

In response, many jurisdictions have reformed their procedures. Line-ups are now frequently administered by officers unaware of who the suspect is, witnesses are told that the offender may not be present, and their level of certainty is recorded immediately, before feedback can inflate it. Some researchers also argue that the first, spontaneous identification is more reliable than later ones, since repeated questioning gives the mind opportunities to blend genuine memory with suggestion.

It would be mistaken, however, to conclude that memory is simply worthless. In most everyday circumstances, the gist of what we remember is accurate, and the reconstructive nature of memory serves a purpose. It allows us to generalise from past experience, to imagine future situations, and to avoid being burdened by every trivial detail. Indeed, some scientists argue that the same system that produces false memories is the one that makes planning and creativity possible. The flaws, in other words, may be the price of a remarkably flexible faculty.

The practical lesson is a measured scepticism. When an account is crucial, whether in a legal case, a historical inquiry, or a family dispute, it should be corroborated by independent evidence such as documents, recordings, or other witnesses. And when our own memory insists on a version of events that others contest, humility is warranted. Feeling certain is not the same as being right, and recognising that distinction may be among the most useful habits a thoughtful person can cultivate.

t: The Quiet Revolution in Urban Planning
p: For much of the twentieth century, the dominant image of the modern city was shaped by the automobile. Planners separated homes, offices, and shops into distinct zones, connected by wide roads, on the assumption that residents would drive between them. The outcome in many countries was a landscape of sprawling suburbs, where even a loaf of bread required a car journey. Only in recent decades has this model been seriously questioned, and a quiet revolution in urban planning is now under way.

At the centre of the new thinking is the idea of the compact, mixed-use neighbourhood, sometimes summarised as the 'fifteen-minute city', in which most daily needs, such as schools, shops, parks, and health services, can be reached on foot or by bicycle within a quarter of an hour. Proponents argue that this arrangement reduces emissions, saves time, and strengthens local communities, since people who walk past one another every day are more likely to form relationships. It also benefits those who cannot drive, including children, the elderly, and people on low incomes.

Achieving this vision is considerably harder than describing it. Existing cities cannot be rebuilt from scratch, and planners must work within a dense mixture of historic buildings, private property, and entrenched habits. Much of the effort therefore consists of modest adjustments: relaxing zoning rules to allow small shops in residential streets, converting unused offices into flats, and reclaiming parking spaces for trees and cafés. Individually, these measures appear unremarkable; collectively, they can alter the character of a district.

Resistance is common, and not always irrational. Shopkeepers worry that reducing parking will drive customers away, although studies in a number of cities suggest that pedestrians and cyclists spend more in aggregate than drivers who visit less often. Residents of established neighbourhoods fear that increased density will bring noise, congestion, and a change in the appearance of their streets. There is also a legitimate concern about gentrification: as an area becomes more attractive, rents rise, and the long-standing residents whom the improvements were meant to serve may be displaced.

For this reason, many urbanists insist that environmental goals cannot be separated from questions of fairness. A neighbourhood with excellent amenities but no affordable housing merely relocates the problem. Some municipalities have attempted to address it by requiring developers to reserve a share of new apartments at controlled prices, by supporting community land trusts, or by directing investment first toward the districts that have been neglected the longest. The results have been uneven, which illustrates how difficult it is to improve a place without altering who can afford to live there.

Critics from another direction suggest that the fifteen-minute concept oversimplifies how people actually live. Individuals do not necessarily work, shop, and socialise close to home; they choose jobs and friends across an entire metropolitan region, and a city's vitality depends in part on the ease with which they can move beyond their own neighbourhood. A balanced approach, these critics maintain, would combine strong local centres with fast, reliable public transport, rather than treating proximity as the sole virtue.

What is striking about the present moment is the degree of convergence across very different cities. Paris, Melbourne, and Bogotá, each with its own history and politics, have all experimented with restricting traffic, widening pavements, and creating new public spaces. Their success has varied, but they share a recognition that streets are not merely corridors for vehicles; they are among the most valuable shared spaces a community possesses.

If the revolution has been quiet, it is because it proceeds through small decisions: a bench here, a bicycle lane there, a changed regulation in an obscure planning document. Yet the cumulative effect may prove as profound as the arrival of the motorcar itself. Whether it ultimately produces cities that are healthier and more inclusive, or merely more expensive, will depend on whether planners treat the improvement of the physical environment and the protection of the people who live in it as a single task.

p: Few ideas are as intuitively appealing, or as philosophically fraught, as that of moral progress. We tend to assume that our ancestors' acceptance of slavery, the subjugation of women, and the public torture of criminals represents a stage of ignorance that we have since transcended. To speak in this way, however, is to presuppose a standard by which moral views can be ranked, and it is precisely the existence of such a standard that sceptics have contested. If morality is merely the expression of a society's conventions, then the change from one set of values to another is mere change, not improvement, and our sense of superiority is nothing more than the parochial vanity of every age.

Defenders of progress typically respond by pointing to features of moral change that are difficult to attribute to fashion alone. The abolition of slavery, they note, did not simply replace one preference with another; it was driven in large part by the recognition that the interests of the enslaved were of the same kind as those of their masters, and that the arguments used to justify their treatment could not withstand consistent scrutiny. On this account, moral advance resembles intellectual advance: it consists in the discovery of inconsistencies, the extension of principles to cases previously overlooked, and the correction of factual errors, such as false beliefs about the capacities of particular groups.

This analogy, though illuminating, invites complications. Scientific progress is evaluated against a physical world that resists our theories, whereas it is far from obvious what plays the corresponding role in ethics. Moral realists maintain that there are objective truths about right and wrong, independent of what anyone believes; yet they struggle to explain how such truths could be known, or why human beings, products of a blind evolutionary process, should be equipped to detect them. Anti-realists, by contrast, can account for the origin of our moral sense but have difficulty justifying the confidence with which we condemn practices in other cultures and periods.

A subtler challenge arises from the observation that moral progress has been neither uniform nor irreversible. The twentieth century, which produced the most elaborate declarations of human rights in history, also witnessed atrocities on an industrial scale, committed in some cases by societies that were by any measure highly educated. The lesson drawn by many is that moral advance is contingent: it depends on institutions, on the diffusion of particular habits of thought, and on conditions of security and prosperity that can disappear. Any teleological story in which history moves inevitably toward justice is therefore as unfounded as it is comforting.

Moreover, the very notion of progress can foster a corrosive complacency. If we are persuaded that we stand at the summit of moral understanding, we are unlikely to ask what future generations will condemn in us. Historians have observed that those who defended slavery or the exclusion of women from public life rarely thought of themselves as monsters; they were, for the most part, respectable people confident in their rectitude. It would be remarkable if we alone had escaped such blindness. A more defensible attitude, perhaps, is one that retains the conviction that some moral views are better than others while holding that conviction with a measure of humility.

Candidates for our own blind spots are not hard to find. Some point to the treatment of animals in industrial agriculture, others to the neglect of distant strangers whose suffering we could relieve at modest cost, and others still to the obligations we owe to people not yet born. What these examples share is a structure: in each, a group whose interests are real but whose voice is absent bears the consequences of practices from which others benefit. Whether or not one accepts any particular example, the pattern is instructive, since it suggests where moral scrutiny should be directed.

The upshot is a position that is neither triumphalist nor despairing. One may hold that moral progress is real, in the sense that certain changes reflect better reasoning and greater impartiality, without supposing that it is guaranteed or complete. Such a view imposes demanding obligations. It requires that we defend hard-won achievements against erosion, that we remain open to arguments that unsettle our assumptions, and that we recognise that the question of what we owe to one another is never finally closed. Progress, on this understanding, is not a destination that history delivers but a task that each generation must undertake anew.

q.e: If morality is conventions, change is not improvement; superiority is parochial vanity.

p: The suggestion that the language we speak shapes the way we think has fascinated scholars and the public alike for nearly a century. Associated with the linguists Edward Sapir and Benjamin Lee Whorf, the hypothesis of linguistic relativity holds, in its strongest version, that speakers of different languages inhabit different conceptual worlds, since the categories their language provides set the boundaries of what they can think. Few researchers now defend this extreme position, but the more moderate question of whether language influences cognition in measurable ways has proved remarkably productive, and its answer remains disputed.

The strong version encounters immediate difficulties. If thought were determined by language, translation would be impossible, and children who have not yet acquired language, along with the deaf individuals who grow up without any, would be incapable of reasoning. Neither is the case. Infants demonstrate sophisticated expectations about objects and quantities months before they speak, and bilingual speakers move between conceptual systems with little apparent difficulty. Moreover, the popular claim that the Inuit possess dozens of words for snow, so often repeated as evidence, turns out to rest on a misunderstanding of how their languages form words, and is in any case inadequate to establish a difference in thinking.

More persuasive evidence comes from carefully controlled experiments. Russian distinguishes obligatorily between lighter and darker blues, using two separate basic terms, and Russian speakers have been found to discriminate between shades straddling that boundary slightly faster than English speakers, whose language lacks the distinction. Speakers of a language of Australia that uses absolute compass directions instead of 'left' and 'right' maintain an extraordinary sense of orientation, and arrange sequences of events, such as a series of photographs, along an east-to-west axis irrespective of how they are seated. Such results indicate that habitual linguistic distinctions can sharpen attention to corresponding features of the world.

The interpretation of these findings is nevertheless contentious. Critics observe that the effects are typically small, appear only under particular conditions, and often vanish when participants are occupied with a second task, which suggests that language modulates the speed of a judgement without altering the underlying perception. Others argue that the correlation can run in the opposite direction: a community that frequently needs to describe compass directions, because of its environment, may develop the vocabulary for them, rather than the vocabulary producing the skill. Disentangling culture, environment, and language, which are inevitably intertwined, remains a formidable methodological problem.

Perhaps the most defensible formulation is that languages differ less in what they allow their speakers to think than in what they oblige them to notice. A speaker of a language that marks grammatical gender on every noun must repeatedly attend to a property that speakers of other languages may ignore; one whose grammar requires the source of information to be indicated, whether witnessed or merely inferred, cannot make an assertion without implicitly addressing the evidence for it. Because such obligations apply constantly, even slight tendencies may accumulate, affecting what becomes salient in memory, description, and perhaps reasoning.

There are practical dimensions to the question. Translators and diplomats know that apparently equivalent expressions carry different connotations, and misunderstandings sometimes arise from differences that are subtle rather than obvious. In education, there is evidence that children whose language expresses numbers in a regular, transparent way learn to count earlier than those who must master irregular forms. None of this implies that one language is superior; it suggests only that the tools of expression are not entirely neutral.

What emerges, then, is a nuanced picture that neither the enthusiasts nor the dismissive sceptics anticipated. Language does not imprison thought, and the dream of a hidden mental world accessible only to speakers of a particular tongue is a romantic exaggeration. Yet to treat language as a transparent window onto a universal mind is equally simplistic. The more plausible conclusion is that linguistic habits exert a gentle, pervasive pressure on attention and memory, one whose strength depends on the task and the context, and whose precise extent will occupy researchers for many years to come.

All languages share exactly the same structure.
q.e: Categories provided by language set the boundaries of thought.

q.e: Infants show sophisticated expectations before speaking; translation is possible.

q.e: Russian speakers discriminate faster between shades straddling the boundary.

q.e: Effects vanish under a second task, suggesting language modulates speed only.

q.e: Grammar like gender or evidentiality requires attention to certain properties each time.

q.e: Children learn to count earlier where numbers are expressed regularly.

Language traps thought and makes change impossible for us.
Language is a clear window onto a universal human mind.

q.e: Linguistic habits exert a gentle pervasive pressure whose strength depends on task and context.

p: In many cities, a quiet change is taking place in the way people eat. Instead of cooking alone at home or buying ready meals, more and more people are joining community kitchens. These are shared spaces where neighbours meet once or twice a week to prepare a meal together and then eat it at one big table. Some kitchens are run by charities, while others are organised by the residents themselves.

Nora, a 28-year-old nurse, joined a community kitchen in her neighbourhood last year. She had recently moved to a new city and knew nobody there. "I worked long shifts and usually ate a sandwich standing up," she says. "At the kitchen, I learned to make soup from scratch and, more importantly, I made friends." Now she goes every Thursday evening and often brings a recipe from her grandmother.

The kitchens also help people save money. The food is usually bought in large quantities, so it is cheaper, and the ingredients are shared among everyone. Many kitchens use vegetables that supermarkets cannot sell because they look strange or are close to their expiry date. In this way, the projects reduce food waste as well as the cost of a meal.

Of course, there are challenges. Organisers need a suitable place, and the rules about food safety are strict. Volunteers must wash their hands, label allergies and keep the kitchen spotless. Some people also find it difficult to cook in a large group because everyone has a different idea about how much salt or spice a dish needs. "We argue about garlic every week," laughs one volunteer.

Still, most members agree that the benefits are greater than the problems. Cooking together gives people a reason to leave the house, talk to others and try new foods. As one organiser says, "A meal is never only about food. It is about sitting together and feeling that you belong."

q.e: The text covers friendship, lower costs and shared meals.

q.e: Bulk buying and unsellable vegetables lower the cost.
