t: Learning to Swim as an Adult
p: Most people learn to swim as children, but a surprising number of adults never do. The reasons vary: some grew up far from water, others had a frightening experience, and many simply felt too embarrassed to ask for lessons later in life. For these people, standing at the edge of a pool can be a source of real anxiety.

Tomas, a 42-year-old accountant, was one of them. When he was seven, he fell into a lake and had to be pulled out by his uncle. After that, he avoided water for thirty-five years. "I told my family that I didn't like the beach," he says. "The truth was that I was afraid." The turning point came when his daughter started swimming lessons and asked him to join her in the pool.

Tomas signed up for an adult beginners' class at his local sports centre. The first lesson was difficult. He held on to the side of the pool and could not even put his face in the water. However, the instructor, a patient woman called Lucia, did not rush him. She explained that fear is a natural reaction and that progress is measured in small steps. In the first month, the class practised only breathing and floating.

Instructors say that adult learners face special challenges. Their bodies are less flexible than children's, and they worry about what other people think. On the other hand, adults are usually more determined, and they understand instructions better. "Children copy what they see," says Lucia. "Adults ask why, and that helps them to improve their technique."

After six months, Tomas could swim twenty-five metres without stopping. Last summer, he swam in the sea for the first time. "I cried a little," he admits, "but nobody could see because my face was wet anyway." He now recommends lessons to anyone who is still afraid. "It's never too late. The hardest part is walking through the door."

q.e: The first paragraph lists three kinds of reasons.

q.e: He fell into a lake at the age of seven.

q.e: The turning point was his daughter's request.

q.e: She did not rush him; the class only practised breathing and floating.

p: For most of the twentieth century, the idea of a "dream home" meant more space: more bedrooms, a bigger garden and a double garage. Recently, however, a growing number of people have chosen the opposite. They live in tiny houses of less than thirty square metres, many of which are built on wheels so that they can be moved.

Ivy, a 31-year-old web designer, built her tiny house in a friend's garden. It has a kitchen, a bathroom, a sleeping area above the stairs and a small desk by the window. "At first, I worried that I wouldn't have enough room for my things," she says. "So I sold or gave away about three quarters of what I owned. It felt strange, then liberating."

There are practical reasons for the trend. Houses in many cities have become so expensive that young people cannot afford to buy one. A tiny house costs a fraction of the price, and its bills are much lower because it needs less energy to heat. Some owners also like the idea of leaving a smaller carbon footprint.

Living small has disadvantages, too. Guests have to sit close together, and storing things is a constant challenge. In many places, it is also difficult to find legal land where a tiny house can be placed, because local rules often require a minimum size for homes. Couples sometimes find that two people in such a small space need a lot of patience.

Nevertheless, supporters say the lifestyle teaches valuable lessons. "You stop buying things just because they are on sale," Ivy explains. "You ask yourself whether you really need something, and usually the answer is no." For her, the biggest benefit is not the money she saves, but the freedom to spend her time on what matters to her.

q.e: The text gives reasons, problems and benefits of tiny houses.

p: Every night, whether we remember it or not, we dream. A typical person spends about two hours dreaming, which adds up to roughly six years over a lifetime. Yet scientists are still debating a basic question: why? Dreams have fascinated philosophers for thousands of years, but it is only in the last century that researchers have been able to study sleeping brains in detail.

The most vivid dreams occur during a stage called REM sleep, when the eyes move rapidly and the brain is almost as active as when we are awake. One influential theory suggests that this is when the brain sorts through the day's experiences, deciding which memories to keep and which to discard. In experiments, students who slept after learning a list of words remembered more of them the next day than students who stayed awake, which supports the idea that sleep strengthens memory.

A second theory focuses on emotions. Dreams, according to this view, work like a kind of overnight therapy. Because the chemicals associated with stress are reduced during REM sleep, the brain can revisit painful experiences without feeling their full force. People who have lost a loved one or survived a frightening event often dream about it repeatedly, and these dreams usually become less distressing over time.

Some researchers are more sceptical. They argue that dreams may simply be a by-product of the brain's activity, a kind of random noise that the mind turns into stories. According to this "activation-synthesis" hypothesis, the content of a dream has no special meaning. Supporters of this view point out that dreams are often illogical: we accept impossible events without surprise and rarely notice that we are dreaming.

Whatever their purpose, dreams can influence waking life. Artists and scientists have reported solving problems or finding ideas in their sleep, and some therapists use dreams as a starting point for discussion. Perhaps the most sensible conclusion is that dreaming serves more than one function. As technology improves, researchers hope to track brain activity so precisely that the mystery will finally be solved.

o: To compare different explanations for dreaming
To teach readers to remember their dreams
To show that dreams can predict the future
To describe each stage of sleep in detail
q.e: The text presents memory, emotion and random-activity theories.

q.e: Students who slept remembered more words.

q.e: The brain can revisit painful memories with less stress.

q.e: Sceptical researchers question the earlier theories.

q.e: Illogical events suggest random brain noise.

q.e: Health benefits are not mentioned in paragraph 5.

p: Not long ago, painting on a public wall without permission was seen as little more than vandalism. Today, the work of street artists hangs in galleries, sells for millions at auction and attracts tourists from around the world. This change has led to a lively debate: should street art remain a rebellious act, or can it become a respectable part of the art world?

Defenders of street art argue that it brings colour and meaning to neglected places. In many cities, councils now invite artists to decorate blank walls, abandoned factories and tunnels. In one industrial area of Bristol, a series of murals reduced the amount of graffiti tagging by almost half, as local people felt more proud of their neighbourhood and less willing to damage it.

Critics, however, point out that legal commissions take away what made street art special. Part of its appeal came from its risk and its unexpected appearance; once it is organised by officials, they say, it loses its voice. Others worry about a phenomenon known as "artwashing", in which property developers pay for attractive murals to make an area fashionable, only for rents to rise and long-term residents to be forced out.

Then there is the question of ownership. When a famous artist paints on a wall, who does the picture belong to: the artist, the building owner or the public? In several cases, owners have sold walls with the artwork still on them, while artists have complained that they received nothing. Because the paintings are exposed to weather and are sometimes covered over by other artists, they are also temporary by nature.

Many artists accept this impermanence as part of the point. "A wall is not a canvas," says one painter, "it is a conversation. Someone will answer me by painting over my work, and that's fine." Whether it is vandalism or culture, street art has changed how many of us look at the city around us, and it encourages us to see public space as something that anyone can shape.

p: Ten years ago, few people had heard of "gig work". Today, millions earn money by delivering food on bicycles, driving passengers or completing small online tasks, with each job arranged through a smartphone app. This "gig economy" has changed how people think about employment, and opinion is divided on whether the change is good.

For many workers, the main attraction is flexibility. Gig workers decide when and how long to work, which suits students, parents with young children and anyone who needs extra income. Mara, a 24-year-old university student, delivers meals at weekends. "I can switch off the app when I have an exam," she says. "In a regular job, my manager would probably not be so understanding."

Yet this freedom comes at a price. Most gig workers are classed as self-employed, so they receive no paid holidays, sick pay or pension contributions from the companies whose apps they use. If they fall ill or have an accident, they simply stop earning. Their income can also be unpredictable: demand rises and falls, and the payment for each job may change without warning. Some workers find that after paying for fuel, insurance and repairs, their real hourly pay is below the minimum wage.

Governments are struggling to respond. In some countries, courts have ruled that certain gig workers should be treated as employees, which would entitle them to basic rights. Companies argue that such rules would force them to cut jobs and raise prices, and that workers themselves value independence. Surveys show that opinions differ: many people appreciate the freedom, but a majority also say they would like more protection.

Economists suggest that the answer may lie in a middle path, such as a flexible contract that still provides basic security. Whatever solution is found, the gig economy is unlikely to disappear. As more of our lives move online, the question is not whether this type of work will exist, but how fairly it will be organised.

p: If you enjoyed an apple, a cup of coffee or a handful of almonds today, you can thank a bee. About one third of the food we eat depends on pollination, the process by which insects carry pollen from flower to flower so that plants can produce fruit and seeds. Honeybees get most of the attention, but thousands of wild bee species do the same job, often more efficiently.

Unfortunately, bees are in trouble. In many parts of the world, their numbers have fallen sharply over the last few decades. Scientists rarely blame a single cause. Instead, they point to a combination of pressures: the loss of wild flowers as farmland and cities expand, diseases carried by small creatures called mites, climate change that disturbs the timing of flowering, and the widespread use of certain pesticides.

The pesticide issue has been especially controversial. A group of chemicals known as neonicotinoids was found to damage bees' ability to find their way home. After years of research and campaigning, the European Union banned their use on outdoor crops in 2018. Farming organisations objected, arguing that the alternatives were more expensive and less effective, but many scientists welcomed the decision as a sign that evidence can influence policy.

Ordinary people can help, too. Planting flowers on balconies, leaving part of a garden uncut and avoiding chemical sprays all give bees food and shelter. Some cities have turned roofs into meadows, and a few have even created "bee corridors" of flowering plants along roads. Beekeeping has become popular as well, though experts warn that keeping hives in a city without enough flowers can actually harm wild species by creating competition for food.

Protecting bees is not only about saving an insect. It is about protecting the systems that feed us. Without pollinators, farmers would have to move pollen by hand, as already happens in parts of China, at enormous cost. As one ecologist puts it, "Looking after bees is the cheapest insurance policy humanity has."

q.q: What is the main purpose of the text?

t: The True Price of Fast Fashion
p: A T-shirt that costs less than a sandwich has become an ordinary sight on the high street. Fast fashion, the business model of producing inexpensive clothes in response to rapidly changing trends, has transformed the industry. Where designers once showed two collections a year, some brands now introduce thousands of new styles every week. For shoppers, the result is a seemingly endless supply of affordable novelty; for the planet and for the people who make the clothes, the picture is considerably less attractive.

The environmental toll is substantial. The fashion industry is estimated to account for around ten per cent of global carbon emissions, more than international flights and shipping combined. Producing a single cotton shirt can require thousands of litres of water, and the dyes used in textile factories frequently pollute rivers in the countries where manufacturing is concentrated. Synthetic fabrics such as polyester add a further problem: each wash releases microscopic plastic fibres that eventually find their way into the oceans.

The human cost is equally troubling. To keep prices low, brands often outsource production to countries where wages are minimal and regulations are weakly enforced. The 2013 collapse of the Rana Plaza factory in Bangladesh, which killed more than a thousand garment workers, exposed how unsafe conditions can be. Although the disaster prompted some reforms, campaigners maintain that many workers still earn too little to live decently, and that brands are reluctant to accept responsibility for their suppliers.

Consumers are not blameless, but placing the burden solely on them is misleading. Surveys indicate that a large share of shoppers claim to care about sustainability, yet few change their habits, partly because ethical alternatives are expensive and information is often vague. Terms such as "eco-friendly" or "conscious" are rarely regulated, which allows companies to engage in what critics call "greenwashing": promoting a modest environmental initiative to distract from damaging practices elsewhere.

Proposed solutions range from the individual to the systemic. Buying fewer, better-made items, repairing garments and choosing second-hand clothing can reduce personal impact, and the resale market is growing rapidly. More ambitious ideas include legislation that obliges companies to disclose their supply chains, taxes on non-recyclable textiles, and "extended producer responsibility" schemes that make brands pay for the disposal of what they sell. Whether such measures can succeed against an industry that thrives on volume remains an open question, but it is increasingly difficult to argue that the true price of a cheap shirt is the one printed on the label.

p: In 1955, an American anaesthetist named Henry Beecher published a paper that would reshape medical thinking. Reviewing fifteen studies, he noticed that around a third of patients improved after receiving a treatment with no active ingredient, such as a sugar pill or an injection of salt water. This phenomenon, called the placebo effect, has since been demonstrated in conditions ranging from pain and depression to Parkinson's disease, and it continues to puzzle researchers.

The mechanism appears to involve expectation. When a person believes that a treatment will work, the brain can release natural painkillers called endorphins, and brain scans show measurable changes in activity. Importantly, the effect is not simply imagination: patients report real relief, and in some cases physical symptoms improve. The strength of a placebo varies with its presentation. Large pills work better than small ones, injections outperform tablets, and expensive brands seem more effective than cheaper but identical versions.

The ritual of care matters as well. Studies show that patients treated by a warm, attentive doctor respond better than those seen by a distant one, even when the treatment is identical. This suggests that part of what we call healing is relational: being listened to and reassured changes how we experience illness. Some researchers argue that a significant portion of the benefit attributed to certain therapies may stem from context rather than from the therapy itself.

The placebo effect presents doctors with an ethical dilemma. Prescribing a treatment that is known to be inert seems to involve deception, and deception undermines the trust on which medicine depends. Remarkably, a handful of trials have found that placebos can work even when patients are told openly that the pills contain no medicine. In one study of people with irritable bowel syndrome, those who knowingly took placebos reported greater improvement than those who received no treatment, although the sample was small and the results require replication.

Critics caution against exaggerating the phenomenon. Much of the apparent improvement in early studies, they note, may reflect natural recovery or the tendency of symptoms to fluctuate, rather than the pill's influence. Placebos cannot shrink tumours or cure infections, and their effects on subjective experiences such as pain are easier to detect than on measurable markers of disease. The most defensible conclusion is that placebo responses are genuine but limited, and that they offer a reminder that the mind and body are not separate systems. For medicine, the challenge lies in harnessing context, communication and expectation without compromising honesty.

p: Few people alive today have seen the sky as their ancestors did. For most of human history, a clear night revealed thousands of stars and the pale band of the Milky Way; now, in many cities, only a few of the brightest stars are visible through a permanent orange haze. This phenomenon, known as light pollution, is the unintended consequence of a world that has become brighter each year, and scientists increasingly warn that its effects extend well beyond the disappointment of amateur astronomers.

The most obvious victims are wildlife. Migrating birds, which often navigate by the stars, are drawn towards illuminated skyscrapers and collide with them in vast numbers. Newly hatched sea turtles crawl towards streetlights rather than the moonlit sea, and moths circle lamps until they are exhausted or eaten. Even small amounts of artificial light can disrupt the breeding patterns of frogs and the pollination activity of nocturnal insects, with consequences that spread through entire ecosystems.

Humans are not immune. Our bodies depend on a daily rhythm regulated by light and darkness, and exposure to bright light in the evening suppresses melatonin, the hormone that prepares us for sleep. Epidemiological studies have linked night-shift work and bright bedrooms with sleep disorders, depression and, more tentatively, certain cancers. While causation is difficult to prove, the correlation has been sufficiently consistent for some health agencies to classify night-shift work as probably carcinogenic.

What makes light pollution unusual among environmental problems is how easily it can be solved. Unlike greenhouse gases, light leaves no residue; switch off a lamp, and the effect disappears instantly. Much of the illumination is simply wasted, directed upwards or sideways instead of onto the ground where it is needed. Simple measures such as shielding fixtures, using warmer-coloured bulbs, installing motion sensors and dimming lights after midnight can cut glare dramatically while saving energy and money.

Some places have already acted. Designated "dark sky reserves" in countries including New Zealand, Namibia and the United Kingdom restrict outdoor lighting to protect both the night sky and local wildlife, and they have become popular with tourists seeking stargazing holidays. Critics sometimes object that darker streets compromise safety, yet evidence for this is surprisingly weak; well-designed lighting that illuminates paths without blinding drivers appears to be at least as effective as indiscriminate brightness. The question, then, is less about choosing between light and dark than about using light with intention.

t: Do Students Learn Better After Sleep?
p: A growing body of research suggests that sleep plays a central role in learning. In one widely cited experiment, two groups of students studied the same list of words. One group slept normally that night, while the other stayed awake. When tested two days later, the rested group recalled roughly a fifth more words, even though both groups had slept equally well on the second night.

Researchers attribute this difference to a process known as memory consolidation, during which the brain strengthens newly formed connections. However, the authors are careful not to overstate their findings. The sample consisted of only forty undergraduates, all of whom were recruited from a single university, and the task itself was highly artificial. It remains unclear whether the effect would be as pronounced for complex skills such as writing an essay or solving mathematical problems.

Despite these limitations, the results have already influenced policy debates. Several schools have experimented with later start times, and early reports indicate modest improvements in attendance. Yet critics point out that such changes may owe as much to other factors, including teacher enthusiasm, as to extra sleep. Most specialists therefore regard the conclusions as tentative until larger studies have replicated the original results.

t: The Hidden Cost of Cheap Delivery
p: Few consumers stop to consider what happens between clicking a button and finding a parcel on their doorstep. Yet the rapid growth of next-day delivery has created what economists call an externality: a cost that falls on people who had no part in the transaction. Delivery vans double-park in narrow streets, adding to congestion, while the emissions they produce affect the air that everyone breathes.

Retailers argue that customers demand speed and that companies are simply responding to the market. This explanation is only partly convincing. Fast delivery is frequently offered free of charge precisely because firms compete for customers, which means that buyers never see the true price of their choice. Had they done so, many might well opt for slower, cheaper options.

Some city councils are therefore considering a small levy on rapid deliveries, with the revenue going towards cycle lanes and electric vehicle charging points. Supporters believe that such a measure would give shoppers an incentive to plan ahead. Opponents warn that the cost would be passed on to lower-income households, who depend most on home delivery. Whether a charge could curb congestion without penalising vulnerable groups remains an open question.

p: It is tempting to think of a language as a fixed system that is gradually spoiled by careless speakers. Linguists, however, take a very different view. Change is not a sign of decay but an inevitable feature of any language that is actually used, and it has been documented in every community that has ever been studied.

Some changes begin with a small group. A new pronunciation may spread because it is associated with a group that has prestige, for instance young city dwellers or well-known broadcasters. Others result from contact between languages: English has borrowed so extensively from French, Norse and Latin that a modern speaker can express the same idea in several different registers.

Attempts to halt change have rarely succeeded. Academies founded to protect national languages have issued dictionaries and rules, yet ordinary speakers have gone on innovating. This does not mean that standards are pointless; clear conventions help writers communicate across regions. But a standard is best seen as a useful agreement at one moment in time rather than a permanent law.

t: The Quiet Return of Urban Bees
p: Cities are not usually thought of as good places for wildlife, yet bees seem to be thriving in many of them. In London, rooftop hives have multiplied over the past decade, and some beekeepers report that their urban colonies produce more honey than those in the countryside.

The reason is partly a matter of food. Intensive farming has reduced the variety of flowers in rural areas, while city gardens, parks and balconies offer plants that bloom at different times of the year. Warmer temperatures in cities also allow bees to forage for longer.

Not everyone is delighted, however. Some ecologists worry that large numbers of honeybees may compete with wild species for limited food. They suggest that planting more flowers would help wild bees more than adding hives. The debate shows that good intentions do not always lead to good results.

p: Online learning grew quickly in recent years, and many students now attend lessons from their bedrooms. Supporters say that it saves travel time, lets people study at their own pace and gives access to teachers from around the world.

Some studies find that learners retain less information from a screen than from a printed page, partly because notifications and other distractions interrupt their concentration. Others show that well-designed online courses with regular feedback can be just as effective as classroom teaching.

Many universities are therefore moving towards blended models that combine online material with face-to-face seminars. The idea is to use technology where it works best, such as for lectures and practice quizzes, and to keep discussion and hands-on work in the classroom.

p: It is easy to envy people with extraordinary memories. Yet the few documented cases of individuals who forget almost nothing suggest that perfect recall comes at a price. Such people often report that trivial details intrude on their thoughts constantly, making it hard to concentrate or to see the bigger picture.

Psychologists argue that forgetting is not simply a failure of the brain but an adaptive feature. By letting go of information that is unlikely to be useful, the mind can prioritise what matters and avoid being overwhelmed. Memories that are rarely retrieved fade, while those that are linked to emotion or repeated experience remain strong.

This view has practical consequences. Students who try to memorise everything often perform worse than those who review selectively, and workers who record every conversation may spend more time searching than thinking. In an age of unlimited digital storage, the real skill may lie not in remembering more, but in deciding what deserves to be remembered.

On Saturday, there are stalls with local food, handmade toys and flowers. My grandmother always sells her homemade jam, and she usually runs out of it by noon. In the evening, there is a concert in the square, and the whole crowd sings together, even if they don't know the words.

The festival ends on Sunday with a picnic by the river. Families bring blankets and share their food with their neighbours. I like this tradition because it makes the town feel like one big family. If you are ever in the area in April, you should come and see it.

p: I had never travelled by plane before, so I was both excited and afraid when my family went to Antalya last summer. We arrived at the airport three hours early, because my father hates being late.

During take-off, I held the armrest tightly. After a few minutes, however, the plane was in the clouds, and I started to relax.

The view was incredible: the sea looked like a blue carpet, and the cars were tiny. The landing was smooth, and everyone clapped. "Was it that terrible?" my father asked. I answered that I wanted to fly again as soon as possible.

t: The True Cost of Fast Fashion
p: A T-shirt for the price of a sandwich sounds like a bargain, but few shoppers stop to ask how it can possibly be so cheap. Fast fashion, the business model that produces trendy clothes at very low prices, depends on speed and volume: some brands now release thousands of new designs every week.

The consequences are considerable. Producing a single cotton T-shirt can require around two and a half thousand litres of water, and synthetic fabrics release tiny plastic fibres every time they are washed. Meanwhile, the average garment is worn only a handful of times before it is thrown away, and much of it ends up in landfill.

There are also human costs. In order to keep prices down, many companies buy from factories where workers earn very little and conditions can be unsafe. Because supply chains are so long and complicated, even well-meaning shoppers find it difficult to know who made their clothes.

Encouragingly, attitudes are beginning to change. Second-hand shops and online resale platforms are growing rapidly, and some young people proudly describe themselves as "thrifters". Experts suggest that the most sustainable garment is the one already in your wardrobe, so buying fewer, better items and wearing them for longer may be the simplest solution of all.

p: In cities where space is expensive, it is surprising to see lettuces growing between the chimneys. Yet rooftop gardens are becoming increasingly common, from restaurants that grow their own herbs to apartment blocks with vegetable beds on the roof.

The benefits go beyond fresh produce. Plants absorb heat, so a green roof can keep a building cooler in summer and warmer in winter, reducing the cost of air conditioning and heating. They also soak up rainwater, which helps cities cope with heavy storms, and they provide a home for insects such as bees.

There are practical difficulties, however. A garden of soil and water is heavy, so the building must be strong enough to support it. Winds can be fierce at that height, and a high yield requires careful watering. For these reasons, many projects begin with lightweight containers rather than deep beds.

Perhaps the greatest value is social. In one neighbourhood, residents who had never spoken to each other started to meet on the roof every weekend. They now share the harvest, swap recipes and organise summer parties. As one gardener told a reporter, "We came for the tomatoes, but we stayed for the people."

p: Last month, I put my phone in a drawer for a whole weekend. I had read an article about "digital detox", and I was curious to see whether I could survive without my devices for forty-eight hours. The answer, it turned out, was complicated.

The first morning was strange. I kept reaching for my pocket, and I felt a kind of restlessness I could not explain. Without notifications, the day seemed much longer. But by the afternoon, I had started a book I had been ignoring for months, and I noticed that I was able to read for an hour without stopping.

Not everything was easy. I missed several messages from friends, and my sister, who could not reach me, became quite worried. Without a map, I also got lost on the way to a café, and I had to ask a stranger for directions, something I had not done in years.

Would I do it again? Probably, but not completely. Instead of cutting myself off, I have decided to set boundaries: no phone at meals, no notifications after nine in the evening and one phone-free day a month. Technology is useful, but it should serve us, not the other way round.

p: In many cultures, failure is considered something to hide. Students are rewarded for correct answers, and a bad mark can feel like a personal disaster. Yet researchers who study achievement increasingly argue that the fear of failure may be doing more harm than failure itself.

One university has started an unusual experiment: a "failure CV", on which students list the projects that did not work out, the jobs they were refused and the exams they did not pass. Alongside each entry, they write what they learnt. The idea is not to feel sad about the past, but to show that setbacks are a normal part of any career.

Psychologists describe a quality called resilience, the ability to recover after a difficulty. According to their research, resilient people do not avoid mistakes; they treat them as information. When something goes wrong, they ask, "What can I change?" rather than "What is wrong with me?"

This does not mean that we should look for failure. But perfectionism, the belief that everything must be done without error, can stop people from trying new things at all. As the saying goes, a ship is safe in the harbour, but that is not what ships are for.

p: We had been looking forward to our holiday in the mountains for months. The forecast said sunshine all week, so we packed shorts, sun cream and hats. When we arrived at the little cabin on Saturday, however, it was pouring with rain.

To my surprise, it turned out to be fun. We played until midnight, and Mum, who nobody expected to win, beat us all. On Wednesday, we put on raincoats and went for a walk anyway. We jumped in puddles, found mushrooms and returned home soaked but laughing.

On Thursday, the sun finally came out. We climbed to the top of the hill and had a picnic. People often ask if the holiday was spoiled by the weather. I tell them it was one of the best we have ever had, because we learnt how to make the best of every situation.

p: Every summer, my father's family gathers at my grandparents' house in the countryside. It is not a small event: more than forty relatives come, from babies to my great-aunt, who is ninety-one years old.

The morning is always busy. The women cook huge pots of food in the kitchen, while the men put tables and chairs under the apple trees. Children run around, and my little cousins usually fall into the stream at least once. My job is to take photographs of everybody, which is not easy when nobody stays still.

After lunch, my grandfather brings out an old photo album. We look at pictures of my parents when they were children, and everyone laughs at their funny clothes. My great-aunt tells stories about the village sixty years ago, when there was no electricity, and the young ones listen carefully.

In the evening, my grandfather makes a short speech and lifts his glass. "To the family," he says, "and to the next generation." I look around the table at all the faces and feel lucky. I know that, wherever I live in the future, this is the place I will always come back to.

p: On Monday morning, Zeynep walked through the gates of her new school feeling very nervous. Her family had moved to a different city, and she did not know anybody. Her heart was beating so fast that she could hardly breathe.

p: One cold evening in November, Kerem was walking home from work when he noticed something dark on the pavement. It was a brown leather wallet. He looked around, but the street was empty.

p: My grandfather decided to learn to ride a bicycle at the age of sixty-eight. When he told us, we thought he was joking. He had lived all his life in a village in the mountains, where people travelled by donkey or on foot, and he had never even sat on a bike.

My brother and I offered to teach him in the empty car park near our house. Grandfather put on a helmet that was far too small, and we held the back of the seat. At first, he wobbled so much that he fell off after three metres. "It's harder than it looks," he said, laughing.

We practised every evening for two weeks. Slowly, he learnt that the secret is not to look at the ground, but straight ahead, and to keep pedalling. On the twelfth day, I let go of the seat without telling him. He rode twenty metres alone before he noticed!

Today, Grandfather cycles to the market every Saturday. Our neighbours wave when they see him, and he waves back with a big smile. "You are never too old to learn," he tells everybody. We are very proud of him.

t: A Day at the Animal Shelter
p: Every other Saturday, I work as a volunteer at an animal shelter on the edge of our town. The shelter looks after about sixty dogs and cats, most of which were found as strays on the street.

My day begins at nine. First, I help to feed the animals and clean their cages. Then I take the dogs for a walk in the field behind the shelter. They are always very excited, and some of them pull so hard that I almost fall over!

In the afternoon, I sit with the cats. Many of them are shy because they have been treated badly. I talk to them quietly and wait until they come to me. It can take weeks, but it is wonderful when a cat finally climbs onto your lap.

The best day is when an animal is adopted. Last week, a family took home a little brown dog called Pepper. Everyone at the shelter clapped as they left. I was happy for him, but I admit I had tears in my eyes.

p: My old phone finally died last week. The screen had been cracked for months, and the battery lasted only two hours. I knew I needed a new one, but I had no idea which to choose, because there are so many different models.

First, I asked my friends. Everyone recommended something different, and each of them said that their own phone was the best. Then I read some reviews online and made a list of the features I really needed: a good camera, a long-lasting battery and a reasonable price.

I went to three shops to compare prices. In the first, a salesman tried to persuade me to buy the most expensive model, which I did not need. In the second, the staff were more helpful, and they explained the difference between a contract and paying all at once. In the third, I found exactly what I wanted at a discount.

I paid, took my new phone home and spent the evening copying my photos. It works perfectly, and I am glad I did not rush. My advice: decide what you need before you go shopping, and do not let anybody sell you more than that.

p: Moving to another country is exciting, but nearly everyone who does so feels homesick at some point. For Ali, who came to Germany to study engineering, it started in the third week. The novelty had worn off, the weather was grey, and he missed his mother's cooking more than he had expected.

Psychologists explain that homesickness is a normal part of what is called culture shock. At first, everything seems new and interesting. Later, small differences, such as different meal times, unfamiliar customs or the language itself, can feel tiring, and people long for the familiar.

Ali tried several things. He called his family every Sunday, but he found that talking to them too often only made him sadder. What really helped was building a routine in his new city: a morning walk, a weekly football match and cooking Turkish dishes with two classmates who loved them.

Experts agree that it takes time, usually a few months, to adapt. They advise newcomers to stay in touch with home without living there in their minds, to look for people who share their interests and to be patient with themselves. As Ali says now, "It never disappears completely, but it becomes a small, warm feeling instead of a heavy one."

p: Every year, millions of tourists travel to Paris to see the Eiffel Tower. It was built between 1887 and 1889 for a world exhibition, and it was supposed to stand for only twenty years. Many Parisians thought it was ugly, and some famous writers even signed a letter against it.

Today, the tower is one of the most visited monuments in the world. It is made of iron, and it is repainted every seven years to protect it from rust. On a clear day, visitors who climb to the top can see for more than sixty kilometres.

If you plan to go, there are a few tips. The queues are shortest early in the morning or late in the evening. You can buy tickets online to save time, and you can walk up the stairs to the second floor if you do not mind climbing about 700 steps. At night, the tower sparkles for five minutes every hour, which is an unforgettable sight.
The tower has survived storms, wars and many arguments about its future. Today, it is loved by locals as well as visitors, and it has become a symbol not only of Paris but of France itself.

p: On Tuesday morning, Hande found a pool of water on her kitchen floor. The washing machine was leaking, and it was only two years old. She turned it off, put towels around it and looked for the warranty papers.

She phoned the repair service of the shop where she had bought it. A polite woman asked for the model number and described the problem. "A technician can come on Thursday between two and five," she said. Hande asked whether somebody could come earlier, but all the other appointments were taken.

On Thursday, the technician arrived at half past three. He checked the machine, found a damaged pipe and replaced it in twenty minutes. Because the machine was still under warranty, Hande did not have to pay for the part or for the visit.

Before he left, the technician gave her some advice: "Never put too much washing in the machine, and clean the filter once a month." Hande thanked him and kept the invoice in a drawer, just in case. That evening, she did three loads of washing and felt very relieved.

p: Scientists agree that the Earth is getting warmer. Over the last hundred years, the average temperature has risen by about one degree, and most of the increase has happened in recent decades. This may not sound like much, but even small changes can have large effects on weather and nature.

The consequences are already visible. Glaciers are shrinking, sea levels are rising, and in many regions summers are becoming hotter and drier. Farmers in some countries face longer droughts, while others suffer from heavier rain and flooding.

The main cause is the gas produced when we burn coal, oil and petrol. Governments are therefore trying to reduce emissions by building wind and solar power stations and by encouraging people to use public transport. Progress, however, is uneven, and critics say that promises are not always kept.

Individuals can also contribute. Saving energy at home, eating less meat and choosing to walk or cycle for short journeys all make a difference when millions of people do them together. As one scientist put it, "We cannot do everything, but everyone can do something."

p: Last month, I forgot my best friend Merve's birthday. I only remembered it two days later, when I saw a photo of her party online. I felt terrible, because we had been friends for ten years and I had never missed it before.

First, I thought about making an excuse: I had too much work, I lost my phone, anything. But I knew she would not believe me, and it would not be honest. So I decided to tell the truth. I called her and said, "I'm so sorry. I forgot, and I have no good reason. I feel awful."

There was a short silence. Then Merve said that she had been upset, but she appreciated my honesty. I offered to take her out for dinner, and she accepted. At the restaurant, I gave her a small present, a book she had wanted for a long time.

That experience taught me something. A good apology has three parts: you say that you are sorry, you accept that it was your fault, and you try to make things right. An excuse can make the other person feel worse, but a sincere apology usually helps to repair the friendship.
